title: From Piles of Mobile Games and a Minecraft License to Opening Cafés — What Is NetEase Games Up To?
excerpt: And of course they would never forget the most important one: *Fantasy Westward Journey*.
body:
And of course they would never forget the most important one: *Fantasy Westward Journey*.

Starting last year, NetEase made May 20 of each year its Game Love Day. The slogan — "We never play games with games" — and the tear-jerking brand film that came with it left a strong impression.

At this year's NetEase Games annual conference on May 20, the company announced a string of moves, from a hard push into mobile games to licensing Minecraft to opening offline cafés.

As one of China's veteran game companies, NetEase has always had a good name: on the strength of operating Blizzard's games under license and of self-developed hits like *Fantasy Westward Journey* and *Dahua Xiyou*, it trails Tencent by a wide margin on the numbers but does much better on word of mouth. It also treats keeping an emotional bond with players as a way of running a business.

This conference's theme, "For the Special You," was exactly that kind of emotional card. Let's look at what it actually did.

## The *Fantasy Westward Journey* Series Is Still NetEase's Most Important Game

*Dahua Xiyou* and *Fantasy Westward Journey* remain NetEase's two brightest signboards. Both PC games have lasted more than a decade, and in the mobile era they have become important NetEase businesses all over again. *Fantasy Westward Journey* in particular has barely fallen out of the top spot on the App Store's top-grossing chart since its mobile version launched last March. At this conference, NetEase said the game's registered players now exceed 100 million.

Those 100 million are users NetEase built up over more than a decade, and it intends to hold on to them at any cost. So it is no surprise that, on top of a sequel and a mobile client, a mobile-on-desktop client and a web version, the company is now adding a *Fantasy Westward Journey* cross-platform edition and a *Fantasy Westward Journey* Wushuang edition.

The cross-platform edition merges the different gameplay and art styles of the PC and mobile versions and lets players carry their data across devices. At its core the aim is to pool PC and mobile players together and strengthen the game's social pull. Sociability is a big part of why *Fantasy Westward Journey* caught fire in the first place: you stay for your friends, your master or your apprentice, the members of your guild, even your in-game spouse, and after all these years of making MMORPGs NetEase knows exactly how much that matters to its games. Pre-registration for the test opens May 31, and a limited-access beta starts June 30.

![NetEase clearly understands what matters most about *Fantasy Westward Journey*.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702115446zOcUl8dT4jvA0G1u.jpg-w600)

The Wushuang edition aims more at players who don't know the series. As the newest entry in the franchise, it tries to bring in new players and pull veterans over with real-time action instead of the turn-based combat that is the series' most classic feature but now looks behind the times. Put simply, it is *Fantasy Westward Journey* played like *Dynasty Warriors*, and it is due on the App Store on May 26.

Beyond that, the *Fantasy Westward Journey* PC client gets an expansion pack this summer, and NetEase has signed Liu Shishi as the series' newest spokesperson. The company also announced seasons three and four of the *Fantasy Westward Journey* animated series — after bringing in TFBoys to sing the theme song last time, it has switched to SNH48 for the theme song "Into the Dream" (《入梦》). SNH48 may fit the tastes of *Fantasy Westward Journey* players better than TFBoys did; the group had already sung the theme song for the game's stage play.

If you doubt whether NetEase should still pour this much effort into a series this old, the bullet comments scrolling over the conference livestream will settle it: two hours after the *Fantasy Westward Journey* segment ended, people were still asking, "When does Fantasy Westward Journey start?" They held a kind of rally in the comment stream — anyone who plays the game, post "1" — and took pride in how much the game means to NetEase, sometimes putting down other games in the process, wittingly or not.

## Mobile Games, a Whole Wave of Them

NetEase only began shipping mobile titles in late 2014, but its 2015 results showed net revenue up 94.7% and net profit up 70% for the year, with 53% of the business coming from mobile games. Last November it passed Tencent to become the App Store's highest-grossing game company for the month.

At this conference, apart from a few veteran PC titles at the start, everything that followed was about mobile games. Even the updates to those old PC titles were mobile-related: *Dahua Xiyou* gets a "Hot Blood" mobile edition in June, and the mobile version of *A Chinese Ghost Story* ran a pile of in-game events on May 20 itself.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021154463aMx5TrOtEliqy0w.jpg-w600)

That goes double for the self-developed new titles — most of what NetEase unveiled this year is for phones. Apart from *Conqueror's Blade*, which looked fairly well made, the new games *Codename: S7* (《代号：S7》), *The Great Voyage* (《大航海之路》), *Tank Company* (《坦克连》), *Endless Warzone EX* (《无尽战区 EX》) and *Eternal Civilization* (《永恒文明》) are all mobile games.

*The Great Voyage* can be read as a mobile *Uncharted Waters*, and *Tank Company* looks like a mobile *World of Tanks*. *Codename: S7* (also called *Land of Oblivion*, 《遗忘之地》) is a self-developed first-person shooter, and *Endless Warzone EX* is a competitive mobile shooter adapted from the PC game of the same name. NetEase has, in effect, caught the current wave of shooters and MOBAs moving onto phones.

None of these, though, is the genre NetEase is best at: MMORPGs (massively multiplayer online role-playing games). Sit through the whole conference and you may develop a mild distaste for the word, because NetEase has made so many games of the type that it comes up constantly. That is also what makes MMORPGs NetEase's strongest genre — the *Fantasy Westward Journey* series being the example. Whether it can do as well outside the genre remains to be seen.

*Eternal Civilization* is the more interesting one. It is an MMORPG too, but it sounds appealing: its world draws on ancient civilizations with strong regional character — Egypt, China, the Maya and others — and players pick a region to fight for. The actual gameplay has not been detailed and no test date is set. Just how much NetEase can still wring out of the MMORPG will have to wait.

## Minecraft — Minecraft, of All Things

NetEase licensing Minecraft was, for a while, assumed to be the big news of this conference.

[Minecraft is a game that changes an era](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/25564.html), after all, and it long ago outgrew being a game to become a tool, a way of thinking and a culture. For NetEase to work with Microsoft and Mojang and take the China license for Minecraft's PC and mobile versions is a real gain for its brand.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702115447P6ywfcOzQiD32pGW.jpg-w600)

What disappoints is how little of the conference went to Minecraft. Apart from a mildly awkward trailer, NetEase vice president Wang Yi and Microsoft's representative simply swapped the game's signature tools — a pickaxe and a sword — said a few official-sounding things, and that was that. Wang even had to read off his phone as he spoke.

Truly... deeply awkward.

Maybe the game is not understood well enough in China. To most people, including the ones filling the comment stream, it is just a pixelated game for elementary schoolers, and comments like "why waste so much breath on this game, replay *Fantasy Westward Journey* instead" were honestly stupefying. Or maybe the Microsoft side was simply in a rush: a scheduled interview was cancelled at the last minute, reportedly for lack of time.

So after something this important — a whole conference and a stack of press releases — we still know nothing concrete about how Minecraft will be brought into China. When testing starts, how it will be run, what the plans are: none of it has been revealed.

That makes it all the more curious that NetEase would treat a game like this this way, because licensing Minecraft is a very strange business to be in. Mojang, and Microsoft after it bought the studio, have always kept the game decentralized: no official servers, and players free to run their own. Where NetEase should position its China server is therefore a delicate question.

It means NetEase has to find ways to draw players onto its servers and get them to spend there. Every revenue model rests on players using NetEase's servers, whether NetEase plans to make money selling the software, selling skins and themes, or something else. But a unified server is bound to limit the game's freedom. And NetEase is facing a group of users it has not dealt with before: unlike its veteran players with a decade or more of PC gaming behind them, most Minecraft players are young — some not yet 10.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702115448dgaWXoelYsPryLi0.jpg-w600)

NetEase could also make money selling or renting Minecraft servers. Ideally it could sell technical support, serving customers who have heard plenty about Minecraft but have no idea how to stand up a server of their own — though that has little to do with holding a license.

Either way, the most immediate problem is what to do about players who already own Minecraft. Most of them downloaded and paid for the PC and mobile clients on Steam and the App Store. How NetEase treats these users and brings them in is a question of its own: for players who have already built a world of their own, starting from nothing on a new server would be painful, and close to impossible to accept.

## On Pan-Entertainment, NetEase Is Still Far Behind Tencent

Early in his talk, NetEase Games vice president Wang Yi said of content partnerships: "[NetEase] does not follow hot topics. In bringing in and working on IP (intellectual property), we cautiously seek deep, joint cooperation among content creators in different fields."

Don't rush to praise NetEase's "cool head." Most companies have in fact already come out of the "IP above all" craze of early last year. Everyone sees the value of IP now, and everyone knows that making one property work across games, film, literature and comics — building so-called pan-entertainment — takes ability.

For NetEase Games, that ability comes down to two things: first, how much good ready-made IP it can get hold of; second, its own ability to create, incubate and run an IP.

Its own decent products have already earned NetEase Games plenty of olive branches from good content owners. *Kung Fu Panda* is one example. Oriental DreamWorks was willing to hand what is arguably its most important character and franchise to NetEase to build a mobile game around, which says something about NetEase's mobile development ability.

At this year's conference NetEase announced another film-and-game tie-in: *Terminator 2*. The 3D special edition of *Terminator 2* reaches Chinese theaters this October, and the film's licensor, DMG Yinji Entertainment, has given the official mobile game, *Terminator 2: The Judge* (《终结者 2：审判者》), to NetEase. NetEase will release it during the film's run and promote the two together. Given how well the *Kung Fu Panda* partnership worked, this one should go well too, though the game itself — action shooting blended with role-playing — asks more of visual effects and combat detail.

NetEase also picked up game-adaptation rights to *Tribes and Empires: Storm of Prophecy* and to the Gu Long catalogue. The former is a TV drama adapted from the fantasy novel of the same name, about clans on the Nine Provinces fighting for power and the throne (a bit like *Nirvana in Fire*); it is due on Hunan TV in 2017. The rights are NetEase's first project turning a TV drama into a game. Gu Long needs no introduction, but NetEase's talk of building a "Year of Gu Long" is a bit much — Jin Yong's various works have not done well as mobile games, and a mobile "Year of Gu Long" may be overstating it. Honestly, after so many sects and so much swordplay, fans tire of it easily.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702115448Dua6MwtrdQAcTEnv.jpg-w600)

Landing outside partnerships is one thing, but NetEase's biggest weakness is still that it is not good at running this content. For one, it has nothing like the interplay Tencent Interactive Entertainment gets from four divisions — comics, literature, video and games — which lets it adapt a work more effectively. For another, NetEase has no place where content is born: for Tencent, the novels on China Literature and the original comics on Tencent Comics are a reserve for what comes next. NetEase is more like a processing plant that is still not much good at mining its own ore.

That is not what NetEase is thinking about right now, though. It has not finished mining the value of classics like *Fantasy Westward Journey*. Having set up NetEase Pictures, the company said it would turn these classic works into films and TV series with Tangren Film and Television and Huace Media. It has also cooked up a "Prometheus Project" to get players involved in adapting games for screen. That does not look like a good move: film-and-game tie-ins really do need people who know the work, and players, however rich their memories of a game, mostly produce nothing. Counting on them to write something good is simply too inefficient.

## And Some Strange Player Programs

If the Prometheus Project is a move NetEase was forced into for want of content of its own, the player-facing moves that followed look like currying favor with players for the sake of currying favor.

First is a 1-billion-yuan "+ Plan." In short, players earn points for what they put into NetEase's various games, and the points buy merchandise, game gift packs and assorted exclusive services. The program covers major PC, mobile and gaming platforms and sounds like something along the lines of a Nintendo Account: raise loyalty through cross-platform integration and points rewards. But compared with what Nintendo does, spending that money on a AAA or otherwise high-production title is probably what players actually want, and would do NetEase more good.

The other is stranger still: NetEase is opening offline themed cafés. In all seriousness it has brought in coffee experts and hotel-management people to build a space where players can meet in person, called Yijian. It announced a "100-Store Plan" — more than 100 locations nationwide — with the first flagship store opening in Guangzhou in the second half of the year.

![They are also recruiting player-baristas.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702115449J5rz4KBRidoWjCUA.jpg-w600)

Sipping coffee while discussing how beautiful Liu Yifei, the new spokesperson for *A Chinese Ghost Story*, is sounds like an odd thing to do. NetEase's games are nowhere near the level where they are talked about in public spaces. Blizzard's games might be, but the license for those is run as its own separate system and was not NetEase Games' brief at this conference. That said, if NetEase runs Minecraft well, that really could give a themed café something to talk about — you can almost see a public place where geeks and small children meet. But until NetEase can spread Minecraft culture in China to anything like the level it has reached in Europe and the US, cafés like this are best treated as an experiment.

The + Plan, the cafés and the various adaptation projects leave us a little worried about a company that once won its reputation on its products. "For the Special You" — beyond the warm card, what players would rather see is the NetEase that settles down and makes games, instead of doing all sorts of odd things in the name of being good to players. What players like most, in the end, is a good game.
